title: Steplab is not the thing.
author: Dominic Salles
summary: Dominic Salles reports on a visit to a Steplab hub school, St Luke's Church of England School, after stating his scepticism about the instructional coaching platform. His objections are that Steplab breaks teaching into too many granular skills, that weekly one-to-one coaching is expensive (he estimates roughly 100,000 pounds a year for 50 teachers), and that online systems get in the way of a human conversation. He found the visit impressive, praising the school's values-led decision making, its timetabled coaching with 94 percent of sessions taking place, and the way deliberate practice standardised common routines such as turn and talk, cold calling and visualiser use. His conclusion is that Steplab itself is not the thing: schools should edit the skill list to stay simple and ask whether each technique is the shortest path to students learning more. He is unpersuaded by the ImpactEd evaluation, which compares top and bottom users and offers no progress measure over time, and argues that curriculum improvements and getting students to work harder will matter more than the coached routines.
points: Salles finds Steplab's hundreds of granular skills too complex and recommends schools keep a short, editable list and judge each technique by whether it is the shortest path to learning.
One-to-one instructional coaching is costly in coach salaries, training and turnover, a price he puts near 100,000 pounds a year for a 50-teacher school.
The most impressive feature at the hub school was consistency: timetabled coaching, 94 percent of sessions delivered, and shared routines visible in every classroom.
Spelling out leadership values and applying them to every decision, such as refusing a public-humiliation planner routine, gives leaders a usable decision framework.
ImpactEd's headline gain compares the highest and lowest users of Steplab and tracks no progress over time, so Salles advises focusing coaching on curriculum quality and student effort instead.
quotes: Steplab has hundreds of skills. This is far too many, far too granular. It demands the wrong approach to expertise, which is complexity and lots of small steps. I prefer things to be simple, repeatable, scaleable.
The cost of coaching is a lot. If you have 50 teachers, each requiring a coach once a week or once a fortnight if they are part time, your cost is around £100,000 per year.
It is very difficult to navigate online systems while having a meaningful conversation with a human being.

Steplab is not the thing, according to Harrison. I agree. I mean the individual skills were too numerous. However, you have complete editorial control to change them to fit the priorities of your own school.

Their weekly statistics were 94% of coaching sessions taking place - an incredible figure when compared to other Steplab schools, and indeed I suspect compared to anything you’ve ever tried to standardise in a school.
If you set out your values, each of these can be applied to any decision.
It is the best way I’ve seen for standardising a common language and practice in a school. If you want consistency, this model of coaching does it.
Annoyingly, ImpactEd’s report offers no measurement of progress and doesn’t track the performance of secondary schools over time.
